An offer by law Offer is part of contract negotiations where a party agrees to do or not do something in exchange for consideration. An offer must be stated and delivered in a way that would lead a reasonable person to expect a binding contract to arise from its acceptance. An offer gives the offeree the ability to accept and form an enforceable contract. 

When a valid offer is made, an acceptance by the offeree creates a binding contract. An offeror generally can not retract the offer once the other party has accepted. A court may not find a binding contract regardless, though, if the negotiation did not involve consideration, involves an illusory promise, or if the offeror did not have the capacity to enter into the contract. However, a contract offer can be withdrawn by notification to the offeree of the intent to withdraw the offer before the offeree has accepted. Offerors typically can withdraw an offer before acceptance in any contract negotiation unless the parties have created an enforceable option contract. If the offeree rejects the offer, the offer can no longer be accepted by the offeree. 

An offer can also be made in the form of a counteroffer. The offeree that receives the initial offer can make a new offer of their own instead of accepting the initial offer. This counteroffer acts as a rejection of the initial offer and creates an entirely new offer that can be accepted or rejected. 

Consideration is a promise, performance, or forbearance bargained by a promisor in exchange for their promise. Consideration is the main element of a contract. Without consideration by both parties, a contract can not be enforceable. For instance, if a person used the money to purchase an apple, the apple is the merchants consideration, and the money is the persons consideration. 

Types : Consideration could be a promise, performance, forbearance, or property with legal value, but the economic benefit is not required. 
A gift or gratuitous promise can not be a consideration for they have no bargaining. The past performance also can not be a consideration as there is no exchange. 

Substitute for consideration : A contract without consideration could be enforceable if it has a substitute. Substitutes are promissory estoppel or detrimental reliance under Restatement ( Second ) of Contracts, or good faith modification under UCC. 
Promissory estoppel/detrimental reliance : A contract without consideration is enforceable if the nonperformance of the promisor will cause injustice. Elements of promissory estoppel are ( i ) the promise has reasonable, foreseeable, and detrimental reliance on the promisor, and ( ii ) the enforcement of the promise is necessary to avoid injustice. 
Good faith modification : A modified contract is a kind of new agreement, which changes parties obligations and then requires new consideration. But contract modification made in good faith under UCC is enforceable even without consideration

I am writing to address the response I received regarding my complaint to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) concerning the rejection of my payment coupons by American Express ( AMEX ). After careful review, I maintain that my payment coupons constitute valid negotiable instruments, and their rejection constitutes a breach of AMEXs fiduciary duty, non-compliance with their own SEC filings, and a violation of relevant UCC provisions and federal regulations. 

According to UCC 3-104 ( a ), a negotiable instrument is defined as an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, with or without interest or other charges described in the promise or order, if it : - Is payable to bearer or to order at the time it is issued or first comes into possession of a holder ; - Is payable on demand or at a definite time ; and - Does not state any other undertaking or instruction by the person promising or ordering payment to do any act in addition to the payment of money. 

The payment coupons I submitted meet the criteria outlined in UCC 3-104 ( a ) and therefore must be recognized as valid negotiable instruments. By rejecting these instruments, AMEX has failed to acknowledge their validity under the UCC. 

Under UCC 3-604 ( a ), a debt is considered discharged if a party tenders payment in good faith and the creditor refuses to accept the payment. My payment coupons, which were properly executed and tendered in good faith, were rejected by AMEX without valid cause. This rejection discharges the debt according to UCC 3-604 ( a ). 

Furthermore, UCC 3-603 ( b ) states that if a negotiable instrument is tendered as payment and rejected, the obligor is relieved of any obligation to pay interest on the amount, and the creditor must return the instrument. Despite my requests, AMEX has failed to return the payment coupons, thereby violating this provision. 

AMEXs actions constitute a breach of fiduciary duty, as the company has an obligation to its customers to honor valid negotiable instruments as a form of payment, in accordance with their own SEC filings. By failing to do so, AMEX has engaged in deceptive practices, misleading me as an investor and customer. 

AMEX 's refusal to accept my valid negotiable instruments as payment, without proper investigation or resolution of the dispute, violates 12 CFR 1026.12 and 1026.13. These regulations require AMEX to promptly investigate and resolve billing errors, including disputes over the validity of payment instruments. AMEXs failure to address the core issue of my right to redeem the negotiable instruments and their reliance on an unsubstantiated claim that the payment coupon is not a valid form of payment violates these consumer protection regulations. 

Failure to address these issues satisfactorily may result in further legal action, including but not limited to, filing additional complaints with regulatory bodies and pursuing legal remedies for breach of fiduciary duty, deceptive practices, and violations of federal law. 

I trust that AMEX will take this matter seriously and rectify the situation promptly.

Under Title 12 CFR 1026.10 ( a ) ( 3 ), part of the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), creditors are mandated to promptly credit consumer accounts for payments or other transactions. If a creditor fails to credit a consumers account, it constitutes a significant billing error. This provision ensures that consumers are accurately charged and that payments are correctly applied to their accounts. 

When a creditor fails to credit a payment, it not only impacts the consumer 's financial standing but also may lead to wrongful late fees, damage to credit scores, and undue stress. Under this regulation, consumers have the right to dispute such errors and seek corrections. The creditor is obligated to investigate and resolve the issue, including crediting the account with the proper amount and rectifying any related adverse effects. This regulation protects consumer rights and ensures financial integrity in billing practices Under 12 CFR 1026.13, creditors must address billing errors promptly. Sections ( 1 ) through ( 7 ) outline the process : XXXX XXXX : Creditors must investigate disputes and resolve them within specific timeframes. 
XXXX XXXX : Consumers must receive written acknowledgment of their dispute within XXXX  days. 
Correction : Errors must be corrected, including adjustments to account balances and refunds if applicable. 
Notice of XXXX : Creditors must notify consumers of the resolution outcome. 
Error Explanation : If an error isnt found, a clear explanation must be provided. 
Interim Credit : XXXX credits XXXX be required while disputes are investigated. 
Continued Charges : Consumers should not be liable for disputed amounts while the investigation is ongoing. 
These regulations ensure fair treatment and accurate billing for consumers..

Come this year, and the findings by the Federal justice system, the US Department of Education, that XXXX XXXX XXXX were basically running an elaborate fraud scheme, I started looking into my options. In regards to the two big private loans, one was initially for ~ {$6800.00}, and the other for ~ {$13000.00}. At this point, I'd paid the smaller one off ( the initial principle plus almost {$4700.00} in interest. ) and was most of the way done with the larger ( over the years, I'd paid all but about {$3500.00} off out of the {$13000.00} initial amount plus almost {$10000.00} in interest. ) Still, I wanted to be out from under it. 

Cue the beginnings of the long and arduous fight I've been dealing with since. 

First, I messaged Navient about if there were any options. It took a bit, but they sent me a vague email of " Oh, there's this school misconduct app, check your navient inbox by clicking this link! '' Which I attempted, but the link was broken. 

THen I sent them another message, saying " Hey, look, I got this response to my question, but where do I find the form. Your link is broken. '' The somewhat ugly response was " Fill out the app provided in a previous email. '' Very unpleasant form letter that all but said the word " XXXX  '' in it. Further attempts there got me nowhere. 

I ended up having to search via XXXX to find the application, and that took me to a XXXX XXXX that provided a link to a third party site because Navient was basically making this process as painful and impossible as they could. 

Then I filled out like ... .fourteen pages of application? I cited the specific loan numbers, the amounts, provided the Education Department " Summary of Findings '' in regards to the school, and had to go into extensive detail about how the school defrauding me and them was... harmful. As if being in crippling, inescapable debt wasnt bad enough, they wanted all kinds of personal details about the experience. I told them what I could. I even pointed out that while I understood we were both defrauded by the school 's overblown and glorified ponzi scheme, the feds had determined what the school had done was... well. Fraudulent. That the Federal Government was going to be REIMBURSING the money paid off on Federal loans for those schools -- and given that the federal government can be pretty miserly with cash, that's huge -- and that it felt pretty shady the way this was being handled by Navient. ( Particularly since the feds had to bully them into even doing this much. ) I honestly wanted my loans wiped out ... and I asked for the ~ {$30000.00} back I had paid them over the decade. Or at least a good portion of it, because ... if it was fraud... then it was also theft. They paid the school, but they made way more off me than they lost to the school. 

I submitted the application. Got an email after a few days that they had gotten the application, and my loan was placed in forbearance for 60 days. Over the next few weeks, I received a ton of ads from them about personal loans and the like, but nothing on the application. Then I get a " Your loans are going to be transferred to XXXX '' notice in my email. 

So I keep checking. Nothing has changed. 

This morning, XX/XX/XXXX, I check again ( I've checked a couple of nights a week since I submitted the application ). There, my loan has been updated -- what I owe has been " Zeroed out '' with a rather interesting backdate of XX/XX/XXXX. But there's no correspondence, no email ( and yes, I checked all my spam folders ), and I've gotten nothing in the mail. In addition my account is still labeled as " in forbearance '' for " another 10 days. '' Given everything, it felt shady, so I used their " Chat with us! '' button to get a person on chat. I really just wanted some kind of information. 

I was informed " oh yes, your application seems to be going through the approval process '' and that " oh, it takes a long time to process, so you'll get an email when its done. '' Okay, fair, I suppose, but really lousy customer service in a history of lousy customer service and shady actions ( Like not informing me ever when the interest rate on a loan changed -- sometimes by as much as 5 % from one month to the next, double dipping on taking money out of my account for monthly payments, etc. ). So I inquired if there was any chance of reimbursement on the money paid in to what was essentially a fraud scheme, and i was told " Oh, well, no. No money will be refunded for payments made PRIOR to your misconduct application being submitted. '' Which ... .like... Let 's think about that. Why would I pay AFTER submitting the application? The whole point of it was to get the loan wiped out and seek reimbursement for the financial damage caused by what has been revealed to be a fraud scheme by a school and capitalized on by a predatory lending company -- in addition to the recent decision about XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX and other colleges like them, I found in my search today that NAVIENT/SALLIE MAE has already been brought up in the past for BEING PART OF THIS WHOLE SCHEME -- there was a case in 2022 that revealed internal memos and stuff about how they were basically preying on people with these loans and fully expected people to default, refused to offer repayment plans, yo-yo-ing interest rates , the whole thing.

I informed the person at Navient I was talking to that I would appreciate documentation of all of this, and that at this point, I would be reporting the company for fraudulent behavior, theft, shady business practices, and seeking legal options for this.

At the end of the day, I'm one person, and they've made almost twice as much from me as they paid to the " school '' I attended. For them, $ XXXX is probably chump change... but for me thats a year 's income BEFORE taxes.

And they service millions of borrowers. There were thousands of people from the schools that the ED found guilty of this fraud scheme. If they're like me, then thats millions of dollars that Navient has STOLEN and DEFRAUDED from every day people.

Something needs to be done. Someone needs to investigate.
